entities.summary:
The Progressive Party (also called the Bull Moose Party) of the United States, founded in 1912 by former President Theodore Roosevelt after his split from the Republican Party, was one of history's most consequential third-party presidential campaigns — Roosevelt received 27.4% of the popular vote (and 88 electoral votes) against both incumbent Republican President Taft and Democrat Woodrow Wilson. The 1912 campaign platform — the New Nationalism — articulated a vision of activist federal government, labor rights, women's suffrage, direct democracy, and environmental conservation that prefigured the New Deal by 20 years.

Roosevelt split from the Republican Party because he believed President Taft had abandoned Progressive reform. The 1912 election created a three-way race: Roosevelt's Progressives received more popular and electoral votes than the Republicans, but Wilson won decisively. An assassination attempt on Roosevelt on October 14, 1912 — a man shot him in the chest before a speech in Milwaukee — was met with Roosevelt completing his 90-minute speech before going to hospital, saying 'It takes more than that to kill a Bull Moose.'

The Progressive Party's 1912 platform included federal income tax, direct election of senators, women's suffrage, initiative and referendum, workers' compensation, unemployment insurance, eight-hour workday, and conservation of natural resources — all of which were eventually enacted within 25 years. The party's 1912 campaign is considered the most programmatically successful third-party effort in American history, as virtually its entire platform was adopted, even though the party itself dissolved after 1916.
